concepts.title: Sampling variation
concepts.summary: Why two groups differ even when the change does nothing.

concepts.title: Null hypothesis
concepts.summary: What 'no effect' predicts, so a result can surprise it.

concepts.title: p-value
concepts.summary: How surprising the data would be if there were no effect.

concepts.title: Confidence interval
concepts.summary: The range of effect sizes the data is consistent with.

concepts.summary: Why a small test can miss a real effect.

concepts.title: Peeking and stopping early
concepts.summary: Why checking every day inflates false positives.

checks.question: The dashboard says +2% conversion, 95% CI from -1% to +5%. Would you ship it?
checks.insight: Reads the point estimate only; does not see that the interval includes no effect or a loss.

checks.question: If there is no effect and we ran this test 100 times, would every run show identical rates?
checks.answer: No, they'd bounce around. So no effect means the difference is near zero, within the usual wobble.
checks.insight: Reached the null's prediction from sampling variation on their own.

checks.question: A test reports p = 0.03. In your own words, what is that 3% the probability of?
checks.answer: That there's a 3% chance the new version isn't better.
checks.insight: Reads the p-value as the probability the hypothesis is true: the most common misconception.

checks.question: Before we look at the data, what does 'the new checkout makes no difference' predict we will see?
checks.answer: That the conversion rates are the same?
checks.insight: Expects identical rates; has not connected the null to the wobble they just described.

checks.question: If we split users into two groups and change nothing, would their conversion rates match? Why or why not?
checks.answer: Not exactly. Each group is a random handful of people, so the rates wobble a bit even with no change.
checks.insight: Explains chance differences and why they shrink with more users.
